Myth: If it happened years ago, I should be over it by now.
Fact: Trauma doesn’t follow a calendar. Symptoms can appear or get worse many years later.

Myth: If it had been that serious, I would remember everything clearly.
Fact: It is common for memories of trauma to be fragmented or confused. That does not invalidate the experience.
If the past shapes your present (relationships, sleep, emotions, substance use) or if your current safety is at risk. Look for a professional trained in trauma.

A phased approach is recommended: first safety and stabilisation (emotion regulation, calming skills), then processing the trauma with trauma-focused therapies (trauma-focused CBT, EMDR) and, finally, reintegration into daily life. The pace is set by the person.
Believe them and don’t press for details: they choose when and what to share.
Help them feel safe through consistency and predictability.
Learn about trauma: intense reactions are not “being dramatic”.
Health anxiety (hypochondria) – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Persistent worry about having or being able to develop a serious illness, despite medical checks.
🩺 Health anxiety (hypochondria)

Health anxiety is when normal body sensations are interpreted as signs of a serious illness and the worry continues even though tests are normal. It is not “pretending to be ill”: the distress is real. It often leads to constant checking, searching online or asking for many appointments, or else to avoiding everything.
Constant fear of having or developing a serious illness
Excessive attention to bodily sensations (heartbeat, aches, marks)
Checking your body, measuring vital signs or looking up symptoms online
Repeatedly asking relatives or doctors for reassurance
Avoiding news, hospitals or conversations about illness
Brief relief after a check-up, then the fear returns

Myth: It’s imagination: you don’t really feel anything.
Fact: The sensations are real. The problem is how they are interpreted and the fear they cause.

Myth: One more test will end the fear.
Fact: Reassurance wears off quickly and feeds the cycle of checking. That is why treatment works on reducing it.
When the worry takes up a lot of time, causes distress, interferes with daily life or leads to many visits or tests without relief.

CBT is the best-evidenced treatment: reinterpreting sensations, reducing checking and reassurance-seeking. It can be combined with coordination between the family doctor and mental health services. An appropriate medical check is never ruled out.
Listen without ridiculing, but avoid giving repeated reassurance: it reinforces the problem.
Encourage them to have a single doctor they see regularly.
Suggest activities that distract them and give them a full life.
Other sleep disorders (apnoea, sleepiness, nightmares) – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
It isn’t all insomnia: apnoea, hypersomnia, narcolepsy, nightmares and parasomnias also affect rest.
😴 Other sleep disorders (apnoea, sleepiness, nightmares)

Besides insomnia, there are other sleep problems worth knowing about. Obstructive sleep apnoea makes breathing stop briefly during the night. Hypersomnia and narcolepsy cause excessive daytime sleepiness. Repeated nightmares can appear with stress or trauma. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors) are more common in childhood. Many have a physical cause that needs to be assessed.
Tiredness or sleepiness during the day despite sleeping many hours
Loud snoring, pauses in breathing or waking up gasping
Morning headaches, dry mouth
Frequent nightmares that cause distress or make you avoid sleep
Unusual movements or behaviour during sleep (walking, talking, shouting)
Uncontrollable sleep attacks during the day

Myth: Sleeping little is a sign of weak will or of being “lazy”.
Fact: Sleep depends on health and physiology. Extreme tiredness can be a medical sign.

Myth: Nightmares are just the result of a heavy dinner.
Fact: They can be linked to stress, trauma or medication, and they can be treated.
If daytime sleepiness makes it hard to drive, work or study, if someone sees you stop breathing while you sleep, or if nightmares or night-time episodes are frequent.

It depends on the disorder. Apnoea is treated with lifestyle measures and, sometimes, positive-pressure devices (CPAP). A sleep study may help. For nightmares there are techniques such as imagery rehearsal therapy. A medical assessment is needed; sleep hygiene alone is not enough.
If you notice pauses in breathing or loud snoring, encourage them to see a doctor.
Avoid waking a person with parasomnias abruptly; protect them from bumps.
Don’t joke about tiredness: it can be medical.
Eating disorders across the lifespan – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
How eating disorders can show up in childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age.
🍎 Eating disorders across the lifespan

Eating disorders have no age. Although they are mostly detected in adolescence, they also appear in childhood, adulthood and older age, and often go unnoticed because they do not fit the usual picture. Spotting them early greatly improves the outlook.
Childhood: very selective eating, fear of vomiting or choking, loss of appetite or weight, poor growth; may be ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder)
Adolescence: restriction and fear of gaining weight, binge eating, vomiting or laxatives, compulsive exercise, avoiding eating with the family, mood changes
Adults: binge eating with loss of control and guilt, extreme diets, constant preoccupation with weight and body, secrecy; can coexist with work and family life
Older adults: weight or appetite loss often put down to “age”, linked to loss, loneliness, depression or illness; risk of malnutrition
At any age: obsession with weight and shape, isolation, changes in behaviour around food

Myth: They only affect teenage girls.
Fact: They affect people of all ages, genders and body types. You don’t have to be very thin to have an eating disorder.

Myth: Young children who don’t eat “will eat when they’re hungry”.
Fact: When eating is very selective or there is weight loss or intense fear, see a paediatrician.

Myth: In older people, losing your appetite is normal.
Fact: It can be a sign of depression, illness or an eating disorder and should be assessed.

If there is notable weight or appetite loss, binge eating or vomiting, avoiding food, excessive concern about weight or changes in growth. For children and teenagers, see the paediatrician or GP soon.

It depends on age: for teenagers with anorexia, family-based treatment (FBT) is the first choice. For adults, CBT and other psychotherapies, with medical and nutritional follow-up. For older people, a comprehensive medical assessment. A multidisciplinary team is often needed.
Speak carefully and without blame: avoid commenting on weight or body.
Keep family meals relaxed, without forcing or arguing.
Look for professional help quickly; don’t wait for it to “pass”.
